notes: \cpara{Recalls three influences from earlier posts: the death spiral around ``intelligence,'' technophilia, and the ethics of personhood in science fiction.}

\cpara{Says science fiction teaches a broad in-group, hence the author's email address. The address is on record: from late November 1996 the young author's posts to the Extropians mailing list are signed ``sentience@pobox.com.''}
\cpara{Recalls, with ``I think,'' the young author's first assumption: a superintelligence would know what is right better than a human could.}

\cfact{The archive bears this out. On 22 November 1996 the young author wrote to the list: ``The Powers will be ethical.'' On 2 December ``whether the Powers will be ethical'' was one of the ``post-Singularity'' questions, for which ``All we need to know'' were the answers ``Almost certainly'', ``of course'', and ``consider the alternative.'' For the essay of the same years, see the note on ``My Childhood Death Spiral.''}
\cpara{Introduces the objections from the mailing list, given ``from memory.''}

\cpara{Gives four objections: morality is arbitrary; a superintelligence would seize all resources out of self-interest; humans should be favoured and uploaded first; an AI needs a control system. The archive has exchanges close to the last two kinds. On 8 December 1996 a list member proposed values ``inerasably etched on the newborn power,'' and on 31 December another wanted an AI physically unable to act on its conclusions until trusted.}
\cpara{Says that Eliezer1996 thought all four obviously wrong and demolished them, and that the adult author has mostly answered them in other posts.}

\cfact{The replies are on record. To the proposal of fixed values, the young author answered on 8 December 1996: ``THIS LINE OF THOUGHT IS THE GREATEST KNOWN DANGER TO HUMANITY!'' To the proposal of physical restraints, on 31 December: ``program 'em right, give 'em ethics instead of emotion, and let 'em loose.''}

\clogic{Two of the conclusions, though not the reasons given for them, are close to the author's later view. ``No Universally Compelling Arguments'' (June 2008) holds that no argument moves ``all physically possible minds,'' and names Eliezer1996 among those who hoped an AI would ``arrive at virtue of its own accord.'' The author's 2008 chapter on AI and global risk says of an unfriendly AI: ``you are made out of atoms which it can use for something else.''}
\cpara{Explains the error by Traditional Rationality's picture of science as a fair fight, in which the side with the best arguments wins.}
\cpara{Says finding flaws is easier than getting the facts right; Eliezer1996 was good at the first, and so seemed to be winning.}
\cpara{Quotes, exactly, the eighth virtue (humility) of the author's own ``Twelve Virtues of Rationality'' (2006): beginners win arguments and overrate themselves. The link names the source.}
\cpara{States the lesson: no one else will argue you out of your mistakes. Adds, with ``I wonder,'' that the advice may help few people until they have failed on their own.}
\cpara{Says the adult author takes Nature, not other people, as the opponent, because a human opponent ``just leads to overconfidence''; Nature does not match its problems to one's skill.}

\cpara{Returns to 1996 and restates what came before: the intuition, the easy refutations, the skill at finding flaws and the ``personal philosophy'' behind it. That philosophy is on record from December 1996; see the note on ``Raised in Technophilia.''}
\cpara{Says that no opponent gave Eliezer1996 the full reduction of morality, and counts it against Eliezer1996 that nothing less would have persuaded.}
\cpara{Says the philosophers on the list offered classic arguments on all sides, which Eliezer1996 could knock down, and so Eliezer1996 concluded that philosophy is a wasteland.}
\cpara{Announces the next stage, dated with ``it might have been 1997'': an attempt to prove that creating superintelligence is right. Continued in the next post.}
